title: Water in buildings: what you can drink and what you can't
summary: Which water already in a building is safe to drink (the tap-water heater, pipes, sealed bottles, and as a last resort a clear toilet tank) and which is for washing or flushing only, or never for drinking: heating loops, solar and ground loops, sprinkler pipes, antifreeze, waterbeds, pools, hot tubs and furnace condensate. Boiling and bleach can't take out chemicals or lead, so none of those can be made safe to drink at home.

steps.text: Before taking water from a building, work out what each tank and pipe belongs to: the tap-water heater, not the heating-system tank or boiler (CDC find water).

Leave out of the drinking supply any water from heating loops, antifreeze lines, sprinkler pipes, solar or ground loops, pools, hot tubs and waterbeds (CDC water safe, FEMA FAQ, OSU BAE-1519, California SWRCB). Boiling and bleach leave chemicals in the water, so they don't make it safe (CDC water safe, EPA emergency).
Shut the main water valve so dirty water can't get in from a broken or contaminated main (CDC find water, FEMA 2004).

Water heater: power or gas off, let it cool, close the cold inlet valve, open a hot tap to let air in and drain it from the valve at the bottom (FEMA 2004, Bradford White). Water from the bottom can carry sediment: let it settle or strain it before treating (Bradford White, CDC water safe).
steps.warn: Tank water at 60 °C (140 °F) scalds within 5 seconds (Bradford White): let it cool. Never turn the power or gas on with the tank empty (FEMA 2004). After two weeks or more unused, run a hot tap several minutes first, away from any flame: hydrogen (Bradford White).

steps.text: Pipes: with the main valve shut and the water heater's power or gas already off (OSU BAE-1519), open the highest tap in the building, then collect from the lowest (FEMA 2004).

Toilet tanks, never bowls: take the water only if it's clear and hasn't been treated with toilet cleaners, such as the kind that colour the water (CDC find water). It is a last resort (FEMA 2004): disinfect it before drinking (OSU BAE-1519).

Treat water from the safe sources above if you are unsure of it: settle or filter cloudy water, then boil it for 1 minute, or add 2 drops of 5–9 % unscented bleach per litre (double the drops if it is cloudy or very cold) and wait at least 30 minutes (CDC water safe). Plain bleach only: no scented, colour-safe or added-cleaner kind (FEMA 2004). The water should smell slightly of bleach; if not, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes (FEMA FAQ).
steps.warn: Boiling and bleach don't remove fuel or toxic chemicals (CDC water safe), and boiling doesn't remove lead (EPA lead). Bleach may not kill parasites such as Cryptosporidium; boiling does (CDC water safe).

steps.text: Keep pool, hot tub, waterbed and aquarium water in marked containers for washing and flushing only, apart from drinking water (CDC find water for pools and spas, OSU BAE-1519 for waterbeds, CDC fish for aquariums).

notes:
## The rule

Water that came in through the supply pipe and sat in the tap-water heater or the pipes is drinking water, as good as the supply was when it stopped, so follow any local advice about the tap water (CDC find water, FEMA FAQ). Water in a closed loop, a heating or fire system, a waterbed, a pool, a hot tub, a fish tank or anything somebody dosed with chemicals is not. Boiling kills germs. Bleach kills viruses and bacteria but may not kill parasites such as Cryptosporidium (CDC water safe). Neither removes heavy metals, salts or most chemicals (EPA emergency), and nothing you can do at home makes water with fuel or toxic chemicals in it safe (CDC water safe). Some waterbeds hold toxic chemicals that emergency disinfection doesn't remove (OSU BAE-1519).

For containers and how long stored water keeps, see the Store water job.

## Water you can drink

| Where | What to know |
|---|---|
| Tank water heater | Only the one that feeds the taps and showers, not a tank that belongs to the heating system (CDC find water). Drain it with the power or gas off; never turn them back on with the tank empty (FEMA 2004). Hot tank water scalds within about 5 seconds at 60 °C (140 °F), the preset on Canadian electric heaters, and sediment collects at the bottom of the tank (Bradford White). OSU says you will probably need a garden hose on the drain valve (OSU BAE-1519); a hose not made for drinking water can add lead or chemicals (Cleveland Water hose). Details: [Water heater teardown](#guides/teardown_water_heater). |
| Pipes | Open the highest tap in the building to let air in, then draw from the lowest tap (FEMA 2004). Shut the main valve first so contaminated water can't flow into the house from a broken main (CDC find water, FEMA 2004), and turn the water heater's power or gas off before you drain the pipes (OSU BAE-1519). |
| Toilet tanks, not bowls | CDC says usable if the water is clear and hasn't been treated with toilet cleaners, such as the kind that colour the water (CDC find water). FEMA's 2004 advice calls it a last resort (FEMA 2004), and Oklahoma State's sheet, adapted from FEMA and the Red Cross, says to disinfect it first (OSU BAE-1519). Do that, and skip any tank with cleaner in it. |
| Ice cubes | If they were made with clean water (CDC find water). |
| Liquid in canned fruit and vegetables | Counts as water (CDC find water). |
| Sealed bottled water | When the tap isn't safe, CDC says to drink bottled, boiled or treated water (CDC find water). Full, sealed water-cooler bottles in offices and shops count: see [Water cooler](#browse/devices/water_cooler). |

**Hydrogen in a water heater.** A hot-water system unused for two weeks or more can hold hydrogen, which is extremely flammable. Run a hot tap for several minutes first, with no smoking or flame near it; if hydrogen is there, you will probably hear a sound like air escaping as the water starts to flow (Bradford White).

**In winter,** Bradford White says to drain its heaters completely to prevent freezing whenever a building is left unoccupied in the cold months (Bradford White). Save the water as you drain it: [Drain a house you can't heat](#guides/skill_winterise_house).

## Water for washing and flushing only

| Where | What's in it | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Swimming pool | Chlorine; outdoor pools also carry stabiliser (cyanuric acid). Hayward's recommended levels for a salt-cell pool are 2,700–3,400 ppm salt and 20–30 ppm stabiliser if needed (Hayward AquaRite); pool chemicals also guard against algae (CDC pool chemicals) | Personal hygiene and cleaning (CDC find water). Not for drinking, and boiling, bleach or other home treatment doesn't take out salts or chemicals (CDC find water, FEMA FAQ, EPA emergency) |
| Hot tub | Chlorine at 3–10 ppm or bromine at 4–8 ppm (CDC Legionella). Kept at 25–45 °C (77–113 °F), where Legionella grows best, and hot tubs speed up the breakdown of disinfectant (CDC Legionella) | Personal hygiene and cleaning (CDC find water). Not for drinking, and not made drinkable by boiling or bleach (CDC find water, FEMA FAQ, EPA emergency); once its disinfectant is gone, treat it as dirty water |
| Waterbed | Up to about 1,500 L (400 US gal); some hold toxic chemicals that disinfection doesn't remove (OSU BAE-1519). The vinyl isn't made for food contact and may leach chemicals into the water (Utah DEQ) | Flushing and floor washing |
| Aquarium | Tank water and everything in the tank can carry germs such as Salmonella and the mycobacteria that cause fish-tank granuloma (CDC fish) | Flushing. Empty it in a tub or outside, not a kitchen sink (CDC fish) |
| Humidifier tank | Germs often grow in humidifiers with standing water in a tank (EPA humidifiers) | Flushing |
| Toilet bowl | Not for drinking (CDC find water) | Flushing |

FEMA's list for water you suspect: don't use it to wash dishes, brush teeth, wash or prepare food, make ice or make baby formula (FEMA FAQ). Keep wash water in marked containers, apart from drinking water ([Keep drinking water separate](#ref/reference_sanitation/keep_drinking_water_separate)).

## Never for drinking: closed loops and system water

| System | What's in it |
|---|---|
| Boiler, radiators, baseboard heating loops | Never for drinking, cooking or hygiene (CDC water safe); FEMA also says not to drink it (FEMA FAQ). May hold hydronic antifreeze (inhibited propylene glycol) and stop-leak compounds; black water comes from oxygen corrosion (Weil-McLain WGO). Weil-McLain warns never to put car, ethylene glycol or petroleum-based antifreeze in a boiler (Weil-McLain WGO). |
| Solar water-heating loop | The roof collectors heat a fluid such as water or glycol, which passes its heat to the tank through a heat exchanger (NRCan solar) |
| Ground-source heat pump loop | A sealed loop of buried plastic pipe full of antifreeze solution, or copper tube with refrigerant in direct-exchange systems (NRCan heat pump) |
| Fire sprinkler pipes | Stagnant water, heavy metals including lead leached from black steel pipe, possible microbial growth, and in some systems antifreeze or other chemical additives (California SWRCB) |
| Winterised RVs, boats and cottages | Antifreeze made for water systems in RVs, boats, vacation homes and pools, and used in traps and drains of unheated buildings (Prestone SDS 834, Purdue PrepNote). Don't drink water from any line that has had antifreeze in it. Purdue says propylene glycol, the type used in RV waste-water systems, is not harmful if swallowed in small amounts but is still not recommended for water supply systems (Purdue PrepNote). The ethanol type is up to about a third ethanol and flammable, and swallowing it can cause vomiting, intoxication and unconsciousness (Prestone SDS 834). See [Live in an RV](#guides/skill_winter_rv). |
| Condensate from high-efficiency furnaces, boilers and water heaters | Formed as flue gas cools; can be as acidic as pH 2.5 and corrodes pipe and concrete (Little Giant condensate) |

Car antifreeze (ethylene glycol) is never safe anywhere in a home water system (Purdue PrepNote). The [chemical](#browse/hazards/chemical) card has the rest.

## Lead from old pipes, taps and hoses

- Canada allowed lead pipe until 1975 and lead solder until 1986 (Health Canada lead). Some homes still have a lead service line, the pipe from the main to the house (Health Canada lead). In homes without one, brass or chrome-plated brass taps are the most common problem and lead solder is another source, and the longer water sits in the pipes the more lead it holds (EPA lead).
- Hot water draws out more lead than cold, so Health Canada says to drink and cook only with cold tap water (Health Canada lead). If it has sat in the pipes for several hours, run the cold tap until it is cold, about a minute, before using it (Health Canada lead). That only clears the standing water: the lead comes from the pipes, taps and solder, and the longer water sits again the more it picks up (EPA lead). Boiling doesn't remove lead (EPA lead).
- Children, infants and unborn babies are the most at risk (Health Canada lead). In an old building, give them your best stored or bottled water, and put pipe water through a filter certified for lead if you have one, cold water only and with the cartridge kept in date (EPA lead, Health Canada lead) ([Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters)).
- Garden hoses, older ones especially, can contain lead, and some leach chemicals, more so when heated by the sun. A hose certified to NSF/ANSI 61 and 372 is made for drinking water, and the source says to run water through any hose before drinking (Cleveland Water hose).

See the [lead](#browse/hazards/lead) card.

## Treating what you collect

If you aren't sure of drinking water from a tank or pipe, treat it (CDC water safe):

| Method | CDC's numbers |
|---|---|
| Boil | Clear water at a rolling boil for 1 minute; 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft) |
| Household bleach, 5–9 % | 2 drops per litre, 8 drops per US gallon |
| Household bleach, 1 % | 10 drops per litre |
| Then | Double the dose for cloudy, coloured or very cold water, and wait at least 30 minutes |

Settle or filter cloudy water first, and use plain, unscented bleach with no colour-safe or added-cleaner kind (CDC water safe, FEMA 2004). Follow the bottle's label if it gives a water-treatment dose (CDC water safe). After the wait the water should smell slightly of bleach; if it doesn't, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes (FEMA FAQ). Boiling is the best way to kill germs; bleach kills viruses and bacteria but may not kill parasites such as Cryptosporidium (CDC water safe). Boiling and bleach don't remove fuel or toxic chemicals (CDC water safe), and boiling doesn't remove lead (EPA lead). For lead and other chemicals in ordinary tap or tank water, see [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters). Don't try to treat the never-drink water above: boiling and bleach leave chemicals, metals and salts in it (EPA emergency, CDC water safe). Pool and hot-tub sheds hold strong chemicals that can injure people when mixed, and CDC says to keep them stored apart and out of the wet (CDC pool chemicals): [Shop chemicals](#ref/reference_chemicals/never_mix).
